title: Question 3
stem:
A U-tube contains liquid, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

{{figure:figure_3_2}}

The total length of the column of liquid in the tube is $L$.

The column of liquid is displaced so that the change in height of the liquid in each arm of the U-tube is $x$, as shown in Fig. 3.2.

The liquid in the U-tube then oscillates with simple harmonic motion such that the acceleration $a$ of the column is given by the expression

$$a = -\left(\frac{2g}{L}\right) x$$

where $g$ is the acceleration of free fall.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate the period $T$ of oscillation of the liquid column for a column length $L$ of $19.0\text{ cm}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the given expression for $a$ and remember the standard form that defines all SHM. What does the number multiplying $x$ represent?
Hint 2: Pick out the coefficient of $x$ in $a = -(2g/L)x$ and set it equal to $\omega^2$. Remember to convert $L = 19.0\text{ cm}$ into metres before using $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Hint 3: Once you have $\omega$ in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, use the link between $\omega$ and period $T$ to find $T$ in seconds.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise the SHM signature**
You have $a = -(2g/L)x$. This is lovely because all simple harmonic motion has exactly the same shape: $$a = -\omega^2 x$$ The minus sign tells you acceleration is always back toward equilibrium, and the size of the constant in front of $x$ is $\omega^2$. So here: $$\omega^2 = \frac{2g}{L}$$

Step 2: **Find angular frequency omega**
Convert length to SI units first: $L = 19.0\text{ cm} = 0.190\text{ m}$. Then: $$\omega^2 = \frac{2 \times 9.81}{0.190}$$ $$\omega^2 \approx 103\text{ rad}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$$ $$\omega \approx 10.2\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$ Think of $\omega$ as how fast the phase angle turns, not a normal velocity.

Step 3: **Convert to period T**
One full oscillation is $2\pi$ radians of phase, so: $$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$$ $$T = \frac{2\pi}{10.2} \approx 0.62\text{ s}$$ That is a fairly quick sloshing back and forth, which makes sense for a short 19 cm column.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
The variation with time $t$ of the displacement $x$ is shown in Fig. 3.3.

{{figure:figure_3_3}}

The period of oscillation of the liquid column of mass $18.0\text{ g}$ is $T$.

The oscillations are damped.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Suggest one cause of the damping.

markscheme_points.text: e.g. viscosity of liquid/friction within the liquid/vi:

hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 3.3 - the peaks get smaller, so mechanical energy is leaving the system. Where could that energy go when liquid moves inside a tube?
parts.proper_answer: Damping due to viscous / frictional forces between the liquid and the tube wall (or internal viscosity of liquid, or air resistance).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the amplitude falls**
In Fig. 3.3 the maximum $x$ shrinks with each swing. That means total mechanical energy is not conserved, it is being gradually turned into heat. Any resistive force opposing the motion will do this. For liquid sloshing in a U-tube the natural culprit is friction with the glass walls and internal viscosity of the liquid itself rubbing as layers slide past each other.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the loss in total energy of the oscillations during the first 2.5 periods of the oscillations.
hints: Hint 1: Total energy in SHM is set by the amplitude. Read the starting amplitude at $t = 0$ and the amplitude after 2.5 periods from Fig. 3.3. Remember 2.5 periods means 2.5 times $T$ along the $t$-axis.
Hint 2: Think about how total energy links $m$, $\omega$ and amplitude $x_0$. Maximum speed is $\omega x_0$, so maximum kinetic energy gives the total energy.
Hint 3: Convert mass to kg and amplitudes to m, then find initial energy minus final energy to get the loss.
parts.proper_answer: Initial $x_0 = 2.0\text{ cm}$, final $x \approx 0.95\text{ cm}$ at $2.5T$. Loss $= \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(x_{initial}^2 - x_{final}^2) \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the two amplitudes**
Total energy is largest at maximum displacement and is proportional to (amplitude)$^2$. From Fig. 3.3 at $t = 0$: $$x_0 = 2.0\text{ cm} = 2.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$ After 2.5 periods you are at $t = 2.5T$, which is the trough halfway between $2T$ and $3T$. The graph there reaches about: $$x_{2.5} \approx 0.95\text{ cm} \approx 0.95 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$ The frequency is almost unchanged by light damping, so you can still use $\omega = 10.2\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ from part (a).

Step 2: **Write total energy in terms of amplitude**
At equilibrium all energy is kinetic with maximum speed $v_0 = \omega x_0$. So total energy is: $$E = \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$$ This is very handy because you know $m$, $\omega$ and $x_0$ directly.

Step 3: **Calculate the loss**
Mass $m = 18.0\text{ g} = 18.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$. Loss = initial - final: $$\Delta E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 (x_{initial}^2 - x_{final}^2)$$ $$\Delta E = \frac{1}{2} \times 18.0 \times 10^{-3} \times (10.2)^2 \times [(2.0 \times 10^{-2})^2 - (0.95 \times 10^{-2})^2]$$ $$\Delta E \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$$ So about three tenths of a millijoule has been turned to heat in the first 2.5 swings.
